The reproductive biology of the Black brotula (Cherublemma emmelas) exhibits life-history traits typical of a deep-dwelling, slow-growing ophidiiform. Field surveys in the Gulf of California recorded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 5% [GSI = 5%] at a water temperature of 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C]. This observation aligns with the pattern seen in other bathyal fishes, where reproductive effort is constrained by limited food resources and low metabolic demands. The size structure of collected specimens reveals that the ultimate standard length reaches 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], representing the maximum body size observed in adults. Mature individuals collected during the spawning season showed a consistent size distribution, with the population-level size at first maturity occurring at a total length of 18.8 cm [Lp = 18.8 cm]. These morphometric benchmarks provide critical baselines for understanding the species growth trajectory and its placement along the slow-fast life-history continuum.

Early life stages of Cherublemma emmelas are characterized by a remarkably small initial mass, a consequence of the minute egg size produced by this species. Based on the average egg diameter of 0.4 mm, the calculated weight at birth is approximately 0.0000335 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000335 grams], a value that places the newly hatched larva among the smallest known for marine teleosts of comparable adult size. This tiny larval mass implies an extremely limited endowment of yolk reserves, which in turn necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding upon mouth opening to avoid starvation. The pelagic larva likely drifts in deep water layers for several weeks before settling. In stark contrast, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is computed from the length-weight relationship at 69.4 grams [Wwi = 69.4 grams], illustrating a dramatic increase in mass over the species lifespan. This substantial gain in biomass occurs over a prolonged period of somatic growth, reflecting the slow accumulation of tissue in a cold, low-productivity environment where food encounters are infrequent and energy expenditure must be carefully balanced.

Pubertal development in this species is closely tied to the attainment of a critical body mass that signals sufficient energy reserves for the onset of gametogenesis. By applying the same length-weight conversion, the calculated wet weight at puberty corresponds to 28 grams [Wwp = 28 grams], which is the mass typically associated with females and males bearing the first signs of gonadal recrudescence. This represents roughly forty percent of the ultimate body mass, a ratio consistent with many iteroparous fishes that defer reproductive activity until a substantial fraction of their growth potential is fulfilled. The reproductive strategy is evidently one of slow maturation, with individuals diverting most of their acquired energy into somatic storage before committing to the high costs of gamete production. The trade-off between somatic maintenance and reproductive output is thus finely tuned to the species deep-sea environment, where predictability of resources is low and interannual variability in recruitment success is high.

Longevity is another key parameter that defines the life-history strategy of this brotulid. Under the stable, cold conditions of its deep-water environment at 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], the maximum lifespan has been estimated at five years [am = five years], a duration that is moderate for a fish of its size but relatively extended compared to short-lived species inhabiting warmer surface waters. This lifespan is derived from otolith-based ageing studies, which indicate that individuals accumulate growth rings at a consistent annual rhythm. The combination of a modest body size and a five-year life span suggests a relatively low annual natural mortality rate, a demographic trait that favors a bet-hedging reproductive strategy. Such a life-history profile, featuring slow growth, late maturation, and a protracted adult phase, is well-suited to the stable but energy-poor bathypelagic zone. The data further imply that a generation time of several years allows for multiple reproductive bouts, which may buffer the population against occasional recruitment failures caused by shifts in oceanographic conditions.

As a member of the Ophidiidae, this species is adapted to a demersal existence on the continental slope and abyssal plains, where it preys on small benthic invertebrates.
